desc:
A string can be scrambled with this recursive procedure. If the string has length 1, stop. Otherwise cut it at some position into two non-empty parts x and y, optionally swap them so the string becomes y + x instead of x + y, and then apply the same procedure independently to each of the two parts (each part may use a different cut and a different swap decision).

Given two strings s1 and s2 of the same length, return true if s2 can be produced from s1 by some sequence of such choices.

s1 = "great", s2 = "rgeat"  ->  true
s1 = "abcde", s2 = "caebd"  ->  false
s1 = "a",     s2 = "a"      ->  true
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: If s2 is a scramble of s1, then at the top-level cut each half of s1 matches some block of s2 as a scramble. Which blocks of s2 can that be?

For a cut of length k there are two possibilities: no swap (the first k characters of s1 against the first k of s2, the rest against the rest) or swap (the first k of s1 against the last k of s2, the rest against the first part).
Memoise on (start in s1, start in s2, length). Prune quickly: two blocks can only be scrambles if they contain exactly the same multiset of letters, and equal blocks are trivially scrambles.
editorial: Let S(i, j, L) be true when s1[i:i+L] can be scrambled into s2[j:j+L]. A block of length 1 matches if the characters are equal. For longer blocks, try every cut k from 1 to L-1. Without a swap we need S(i, j, k) and S(i+k, j+k, L-k). With a swap the first part of s1 lands at the end of s2, so we need S(i, j+L-k, k) and S(i+k, j, L-k).

There are about n<sup>3</sup>/3 states and each tries up to n cuts, so the time is O(n<sup>4</sup>), which is tiny for n ≤ 40. Without memoisation the same sub-blocks are re-solved over and over and the search is exponential. Cheap pruning makes it much faster in practice: if the two blocks are identical return true immediately, and if their sorted letters differ return false, since scrambling only rearranges characters.
